title: Nehemiah
lead: Nehemiah son of Hacaliah, a Jewish cupbearer at the Persian court, came to Jerusalem as governor in 445 BC, rebuilt its walls in fifty-two days and pressed reforms on the community. His first-person memoir, with its short prayers that God would remember him, is the heart of the book named for him; later Jewish and Christian writers remembered him as the builder of Jerusalem.

sections.h: Nehemiah in the Bible and after
sections.b: Nehemiah appears only in the book of Nehemiah (the Nehemiah of Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7 is an earlier man with the same name). He hears of Jerusalem's ruin at Susa, prays, wins leave from Artaxerxes I (Nehemiah 1–2), organizes the rebuilding of the wall against opposition (Nehemiah 3–6), cancels the debts of the poor (Nehemiah 5), stands beside Ezra at the reading of the law (Nehemiah 8:9), dedicates the wall (Nehemiah 12:31–43) and, on a second term, enforces the Sabbath, the tithes and the ban on foreign marriages (Nehemiah 13). Ben Sira praises him as the one "who lifted our fallen walls back up" (Sirach 49:13). 2 Maccabees 1:18–2:13 credits him with rebuilding the Temple and altar, finding the sacred fire and founding a library. Josephus retells his story (Antiquities 11.159–183), and the Talmud both honors him and faults him for praising himself (Bavli Sanhedrin 93b).
